analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy collection on consumer loans charging over roughly 36% interest.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change bankruptcy law so that if a lender charged a consumer an interest rate above the lesser of 15% plus the 30-year Treasury rate or 36% a year, that lender could not collect on the debt when the borrower filed for bankruptcy. It would also protect borrowers with such debts from being pushed out of the simpler bankruptcy process on 'abuse' grounds. The bill was introduced in January 2009 and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers overwhelmed by high-rate debt: by filing bankruptcy, they could wipe out balances on loans charging more than the roughly 36% cap, and they would keep access to the standard bankruptcy process instead of being forced into a stricter chapter. Honest lenders charging under the cap are not affected.

how_it_helps.text: Bankruptcy courts must disallow any claim arising from a high-cost consumer credit transaction, meaning the lender gets nothing on that debt in the bankruptcy distribution [S2][S3].
A high-cost transaction is defined as consumer credit whose APR, including fees, exceeds the lesser of 15% plus the 30-year Treasury yield or 36% at any time the credit is outstanding [S2][S3].
Debtors with such debts are excluded from the mandatory 'substantial abuse' dismissal test that otherwise can force them out of chapter 7 liquidation into repayment plans [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lenders extending credit above the cap: payday, subprime card, and other high-rate lenders would lose their ability to collect through bankruptcy, and mainstream creditors that share in bankruptcy distributions could absorb some of that loss as well.

drawbacks.text: The cost does not disappear; it shifts. Wiping out high-rate claims in bankruptcy means other unsecured creditors recover less, and lenders respond to that risk by raising rates for everyone or refusing credit to financially fragile borrowers altogether.
The protection only reaches people who actually file for bankruptcy, so it does not cap rates for the many borrowers who never file and keep paying above-market rates.
Critics of bankruptcy relief generally argue that making debts easier to erase encourages more filings and higher borrowing costs; the bill does not address that objection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers in bankruptcy, the benefit is real and direct: their highest-rate debts are erased rather than partially repaid. The cost is real too, though it falls mostly on the lenders who chose to lend above 36% and, indirectly, on other creditors in bankruptcy distributions. The design is narrow — it does nothing for borrowers who do not file — so it is a targeted relief measure rather than an across-the-board rate cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled it, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Whitehouse introduced the bill on January 15, 2009, joined by Durbin [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-rate lenders kept their bankruptcy claims: because the bill never became law, creditors charging above the cap could still collect on those debts in bankruptcy, and borrowers remained subject to the existing means test.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on January 15, 2009 [S1][S3].

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined Whitehouse in introducing the bill [S3].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Only four senators supported it — two Democrats, one Independent, plus the Democratic sponsor — and no recorded opposition ever formed because the committee never acted.

industries.industry: Payday and high-cost consumer installment lenders
industries.note: Their entire business model is lending at rates above the roughly 36% threshold; the bill would erase their bankruptcy claims on those loans. Its interest runs against borrowers who file for bankruptcy.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and subprime lenders
industries.note: Most mainstream card rates sat below the cap in 2009, but cards and subprime accounts with effective APRs above the threshold would become uncollectible in bankruptcy. Other unsecured creditors would also recover slightly less in any bankruptcy where a high-rate claim is wiped out.
